standard.title: Explain historical interpretations
standard.description: explain historical interpretations about significant events, individuals and groups
standard.prior_knowledge: Students explain historical interpretations about significant events, individuals and groups (AC9HH7S07). They can identify differing interpretations and explain some reasons for them. They have not yet distinguished short-term triggers from longer-term causes within competing interpretations, or used interpretations to describe change in terms of quality, type, speed and impact.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain historical interpretations about significant events, individuals and groups — identifying differing interpretations and accounting for their differences, including how interpretations of cause distinguish short-term triggers from longer-term causes, and how interpretations can be used to describe change in relation to quality, type, speed and impact.

nodes.label: Identifying differing interpretations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify differing historians' interpretations of a significant event, individual or group, and describe what each interpretation claims.
nodes.minimum_width: Identification of at least two different interpretations of the chosen subject with an accurate description of what each claims.
nodes.typical_width: At least two clearly contrasting interpretations identified and described accurately: differing interpretations of the short-term triggers and longer-term causes of a significant event; differing interpretations of the influence of scientific ideas or the status of women. Understanding that interpretations are not randomly different but rest on different evidence or different weighting of the same evidence.
wider: Identify interpretations of the same event from historians working in different periods or traditions (e.g. a 19th-century European account of the Spanish conquest vs a 21st-century post-colonial account) to show how interpretations are historically situated
Map the range of interpretations of a complex event (e.g. the decline of the Khmer Empire) to show that the interpretive field is not just binary — multiple frameworks can coexist
nodes.hinge_reason: Accurately identifying and describing what each interpretation claims is prerequisite to accounting for why they differ. Students who misrepresent an interpretation cannot meaningfully account for differences or evaluate which is better supported.

response_modes.reason: Accurately paraphrasing interpretations requires care — students often merge interpretations, exaggerate differences, or reduce nuanced positions to caricatures. Repeated practice with varied examples builds accuracy.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two different interpretations of the chosen subject
Accurately describes what each interpretation claims without distorting or merging them

nodes.label: Accounting for differences
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can account for why historians have reached different interpretations — including how short-term triggers and longer-term causes are weighted differently, and how differences in evidence, perspective and context produce different conclusions.
nodes.minimum_width: An explanation of at least one reason why the identified interpretations differ.
nodes.typical_width: Multiple reasons for interpretive divergence, applied to the chosen subject: different weighting of short-term triggers vs longer-term causes (e.g. was the fall of Constantinople primarily caused by Ottoman military power or by internal Byzantine weakness?); different access to sources; different national, cultural or ideological perspectives; the historical context in which the historian worked.
wider: For a cause-focused event: distinguish how different interpretations weight short-term triggers (the immediate precipitating events) vs longer-term structural causes (the underlying conditions) — showing how this distinction produces fundamentally different accounts of why something happened

Examine the influence of scientific ideas on interpretations of the Scientific Revolution — and how interpretations of whether it was a sudden rupture or a gradual evolution differ based on which evidence historians weight most heavily

response_modes.reason: Students often say interpretations differ because 'historians have different opinions' without explaining the specific mechanism. Scaffold the reasoning: what specific difference in evidence, weighting or perspective produces this specific difference in interpretation?

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The short-term trigger vs longer-term cause distinction is a genuinely powerful analytical tool that applies across all historical contexts — learning to see this distinction within interpretive disagreement gives students a reusable framework for interpreting historical debates.
success_criteria: Explains at least one specific reason why identified interpretations differ — not just that historians 'have different views'
Distinguishes between at least two factors that can produce interpretive divergence (e.g. evidence weighting, source access, perspective)

nodes.label: Using interpretations to describe change
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use historical interpretations to describe change in relation to quality, type, speed and impact — explaining what each dimension reveals about the nature of historical change.
nodes.minimum_width: Use of at least one interpretation to describe change in terms of at least two dimensions (quality, type, speed or impact).
nodes.typical_width: Historical interpretations used to describe the multi-dimensional character of change: quality (how complete or partial was the change?), type (was it political, social, economic, cultural?), speed (was it gradual or sudden?), impact (how deeply did it affect different groups?). Application across different types of change — e.g. the Reformation as sudden vs gradual, the Renaissance as rupture vs continuity with medieval scholasticism.
wider: Apply the four dimensions of change to competing interpretations of the same event — e.g. the Black Death — to show how different interpretations emphasise different dimensions (speed: sudden pandemic vs longer-term demographic shift; impact: catastrophic for some groups, less so for others)

Examine how interpretations of Polynesian expansion describe change differently depending on which dimension is emphasised — the speed of settlement, the quality of navigational knowledge, the type of cultural transformation that settlement produced

response_modes.reason: Using interpretations to describe change integrates interpretation identification (Node 1), accounting for differences (Node 2) and the continuity-change analytical framework from S05. Invest in helping students see the four dimensions of change as a tool for making interpretive comparisons more precise.

success_criteria: Uses at least one historical interpretation to describe change in terms of at least two dimensions (quality, type, speed, impact)
Explains what these dimensions reveal about the nature of the historical change being interpreted
